newsitem.title: ITALY: Albanians head for Italy in rusting gunboats.
newsitem.headline: Albanians head for Italy in rusting gunboats.

text.p: Albanians fled to Italy on Friday in a flotilla of rusting gunboats as Western nations mounted military missions to rescue foreigners from the chaos spreading through the Balkan state.

At least 14 Albanian navy craft, most of them small patrol boats built nearly 50 years ago by the Chinese, limped into southern Italian ports under Italian navy escort after crossing the southern Adriatic with deserting servicemen and civilians.

The developing exodus raised fears in Italy of a repeat of the tide of 40,000 Albanians who flooded in on rusting freighters in 1991 after more than four decades of rigid Stalinist rule crumbled in Europe's poorest state.

"God only knows how they made it," said a police officer in Brindisi, where 10 of the decrepit boats, many of them intended for river patrols, were stripped of their light arms by Italian police at the port's military docks.
"It took a fair amount of courage for them to come across in one of these," the police officer said.

One of the patrol boats, which had set out from the Albanian port of Vlore before dawn, reached Brindisi with 177 people crammed on the deck, almost all of them civilians including about 10 children and at least two pregnant women.

"We don't understand anything that's happening at home any more. Everyone has weapons in the south and in the north," said one Albanian man who disembarked after police had used sniffer dogs to search the human cargo for drugs.

Albania's former defence minister Safet Zhulali, removed this week when embattled President Sali Berisha agreed to set up a national unity government in the face of armed rebellion, was among those fleeing the unrest in Europe's poorest state.
Berisha's son and daughter, accompanied by armed bodyguards, fled to Italy on Thursday on a ferry from the port of Durres.
Italian coastguards said Zhulalu, his wife and their 14-year-old daughter were among about 70 Albanians who arrived in Brindisi on Friday on the merchant ship Fulgidus.
Coastguards said another merchant ship, the Ambar, had arrived at the port of Bari with about 40 people on board, including young children. Around 20 were Albanians and there were also several Poles.

The U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) in Geneva said the agency was having talks with Italy and Albania's neighbour Greece over plans to set up camps to hold up to 1,000 and 3,000 Albanians respectively.

"We are asking these governments not to send Albanians back if they come in for the time being, because it is a conflict situation," the U.N. agency's spokeswoman said. "We are saying if they do flee, let them in and let them stay as long as necessary under acceptable conditions," she said.
Italy said emergency measures had been taken to cope with any influx along its southern Adriatic coast.

Piero Fassino, a junior foreign minister, told parliament that while Italy had sought to discourage refugees in recent days "it is clear that the decisions that will be taken by the government must take account of how the situation evolves".
U.S. helicopters began ferrying American nationals away from the Albanian capital Tirana on Friday morning.
Italy said it had completed the evacuation of around 1,000 foreign nationals, 120 of them Britons, and some Albanians, in an operation launched on Thursday using military helicopters and navy ships.

Around 900 of the evacuees were picked up in the port of Durres and heading for Brindisi on two warships, the San Giorgio and the San Giusto. A further 93 were plucked from Tirana's main soccer stadium by helicopters including two giant Chinooks.
